utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ruez. You're a policeman by profession; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had a permanent job in the OTP of this Tribunal. You were employed there from 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not permanent in the way that it was a renewal of the contract on an annual basis. It was renewed until 2001. The date, I requested it not to be renewed any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You worked as an investigator for the Tribunal. Did you understand your role to be the role of an OTP staff member who is supposed to collect evidence on behalf of the Prosecution, or were you an objective investigator?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an investigator in the first stage, the first two years, then a team was created to take -- to take the full scale of this investigation, and then I became an investigation team leader. So indeed the task is, among many other things, to collect evidence, and the way to do so has always to be in an objective manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do with the evidence, documents, and data that were in favour of the accused, i.e., that were not in favour or in support of the indictment and the way things are presented in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't come across of more or less any of evidence that could have been in favour of those later indicted. Nevertheless, when in the field in Republika Srpska, when someone has -- had in his possession anything that could connect with other investigations where Serbs were the victims, either I brought these things back to The Hague to be handed over to those in charge, or advised the person to keep what the person had in order to hand it over at the first opportunity to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an experienced police officer, did you notice some developments or events that might have helped to understand the causes and consequences of the war?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal of the investigation I was in charge of was to determine the fate of some 8.000 persons missing after the fall of UN safe area of Srebrenica. Therefore, the investigation, that is to say, started 11 July 12.00, approximately 12.00. Knowing about the general frame of the war, its causes and all the rest, it is indeed something helpful in order to have what one can call the big picture, but it was certainly not any of the goals of this specific investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This means that you investigated the fate of those 8.000 persons. Can we rely on your investigations with regard to establishing facts, reasons, outcomes of certain operations? Such were small executions, opportunist murders, as you called them yourself. Did you come across such things that might be of assistance to us to establish what really happened there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the reconstruction of the events and the corroboration of these events by the investigation, this court has already relied on the results of this investigation on several occasions. For the rest, it's up to any observer to make his own mind out of all this, and the historians will certainly go again at some day, some point, through all what has been said Srebrenica related during all the trials that have happened here and those who are still awaited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at Mr. Ruez's book again. I'm interested in image number 188. This is how we left it off yesterday. That's the last thing we saw yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you confirmed that the thick blue line is the conflict line. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether that was also the border between the BiH federation and Republika Srpska. Was it a border then, and is it a border now?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This confrontation line has also a specific name. If I remember, it was Sapna thumb, because it has the shape of a thumb. It is a confrontation line. I would not call this a border. Now it's a separation line, not a border, as far as I know. I don't follow the politics in this area since I left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, this was accepted in Dayton as the administrative line between the Republika Srpska and the federation. Did you know that this small area was a very hot spot during the war? Muslim forces wanted to break to the Drina River and Serbian side wanted to shorten the front line. So there were very strong attempts on both sides with -- with these goals in mind.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I see no question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you know that this small area was a very hot spot during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew, but I could only see in this an explanation of the reason why prisoners were brought to take some revenge out of them, due to what President Karadzic describes as a hot spot. I don't know about this possible explanation, but since he provides it, why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the front line moved during the war, and do you agree as a professional that both militaries had reserve trenches and positions in the area in case the front line was taken by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could very well be. We didn't investigate the military structures in place in this location. We only focused our attention on holes that had obviously strictly nothing to do with any defence position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you will agree with me, won't you, that it is only logical that a military has at least two military -- two reserve positions lest the front line is taken by the enemy? Do you agree with me that every military should have that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up to any military force to decide what they have to do to prepare their defence lines. I have nothing to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that the Muslim side would have benefitted a lot if they had broken to the Drina and cut off the Serbian side from the rest of the territory, and it would have been more beneficial than for the Serbian force to get to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some make a profession commenting football match once the match is over, so I'm not in that type of activity. I cannot speculate about what would have happened if. We don't deal with "if."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All this was just an introduction into my next question. Will it be reasonable to assume that during those operations there were a lot of military casualties on both sides? You can answer by just saying yes or no. That would move things along much faster.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to what you learnt about our war, would you agree that each of the sides handed victims and casualties over to their families and that those casualties would be buried by the family in a dignified manner, whereas the enemy casualties that were scattered around its territory would be buried in mass graves without any ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that up to the spring of 1993, in the area that was under the control of Muslims, over 1.200 Serbs were killed, and do you know that they were buried in some 50 mass graves that were discovered subsequently, and General Morillon attended the burial of those casualties?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take these figures as you give them. This were not part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But did you know of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew mainly about one grave that was close to Nezuk, Nezuk being indeed the spot where the column of men, most of them being members of the 28th Division, went through the lines. And this specific grave, we indeed considered that it was better casualties, so we didn't even move to a spot to check about it since there was no link at all with any of what I name the extermination operation. This grave of battle casualties was absolutely not relevant for investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This figure was recorded up to March 1993. Did you know that up to the end, up to the end of 1995, the 28th Division killed over 3.500 Serbs, mostly civilians, all of them in this area?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a team working specifically on the crimes committed against Serb civilians by the 28th Division under the command of Naser Oric, who was indicted and who was on trial at the ICTY. I didn't overlap with the activities of this team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I put it to you that 1.250 people were buried by Muslims in mass graves, and as for the other 2.250, they were buried by Serbs in family graves because those Serbs were kill in the territory that was controlled by us. Does that sound reasonable and plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take any part in this investigation, so I take the figures as you put them, and I have no mean to check and I have no will to do so. It was not at all in the frame of the investigation I was tasked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, did you know that before July 1995, the 28th Division lost over 2.000 combatants who had remained in the Serbian territory? Over 2.000 combatants were lost in the attacks mounted by the 28th Division against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that in the month of July 1995, there was fierce fighting in the area when the 28th Division attempted a breakthrough towards Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only during the attempt of the breakthrough towards Nezuk, but also when the column hitting the direction north arrived in the vicinity of Zvornik, one group of the column made a diversion as if they would attack Zvornik in order to ease the process of all the rest of the column to exit Nezuk. So, yes, indeed, we had the knowledge that there was some fierce fighting going on in the area at the time of the same move of these prisoners taken from Bratunac and who went through the process I described during the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that, and please help us to establish the schedule of -- of events. However, before that my question is this: In that area, the war was ongoing for at least 44 months, and there were casualties throughout the period, casualties among the combatants of the 28th Division, before July 1995 and during the fighting that took place in July 1995. Did anybody provide you with enough background information, and did anybody ask you to distinguish between what was going on with the bodies of the Muslim fighters that were killed over the period of 44 months as opposed to the bodies of the combatants that died in the month of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this claim that there was combat in this area for 44 months has been put to a number of witnesses, and I think if you count back 44 months, it goes well into 1991, and perhaps Mr. Karadzic could clarify if it's his case that there was combat going on in this area in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I think Mr. Ruez is able to answer the question having the knowledge. But, Mr. Karadzic, for purposes, please bear in mind what Mr. Mitchell indicated. Yes, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For sure this is something to consider in order not to mix situations and origins of the victims. This is the reason why the sites we have identified and that we later learned through analysis of captured documents of the Zvornik Brigade that we had in fact found all of the sites that had been used for the purpose of the extermination process of the prisoners, where the full number of them, since we found the logs of the drivers who on 13 July transported the security officers to these sites so that they could assess the detention facilities and identify nearby execution sites. We focused only on the graves where we had information that during the days of 14, 15, and 16 July people had been executed on these spots, and a great load of evidence will be provided to the defendant during the testimonies of both Professor Wright, who -- and -- and Richard Haglund, who already testified, I heard, regarding the content of please mass graves and the complement of all these findings by the exhumation teams, the connections between the detention sites. The primary mass graves and the secondary mass graves will be done with full details by the investigator of this investigation team, Dean Manning. As far as the military overlay of this operation is concerned, the full analysis of it was done by another team member who was Richard Butler and who will be able also to put in relation the events with the more general combat ambiance that occurred not far away from these crime scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you establish where Muslim military casualties were buried during those, say, 14 months, and where those who got killed in the fighting in July 1995 were buried?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the goal of the investigation was not to do a mapping of all the burial sites from 1992 through 1995 but only to focus on the crime scenes connected with the fate of the 8.000 missing men from 11 July, 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. How did you get there? Who gave you that initial figure of 8.000?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is simple. It is a big book from the Red Cross that lists absolutely all the missing persons from the three years of wars, with an S, and this book has approximately, I think, 24.000 names and origins of missing places. One-third of this book has only -- has a missing place, last seen alive, Srebrenica, one-third of the entire conflict, and the figure is around 8.000 for Srebrenica. I recently learned that among these 8.000 already yet more than 6.000 that we found in the primary and secondly graves have been identified by name and are missing from Srebrenica July 1995, by name thanks to DNA analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible to confirm by DNA analysis that these persons were killed or got killed in July 1995, and did DNA analysis provide evidence of how they met their death, in combat or by unlawful execution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able, since I'm not a scientist, to explain in this courtroom how precise the DNA analysis is indeed. For sure, the cause of death is not to be read in the DNA of those who have been assassinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, I forgot to tell the parties that today we'll adjourn at 1.45. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good news is always welcome. High time to hear something good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ruez, do you agree and did you know that at the peak of its population density during 1994, Srebrenica had about 37.000 people, and they reported they had 60 -- 45.000 population in order to get more supplies and more aid?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Though I had no possibility to investigate these figures, the general figure I always came across was approximately, if I remember well, approximately 40.000 persons in the enclave, but, yes, there was always the -- the possibility that indeed in order to attract more aid the figures were fuzzy and most possibly raised at a higher level. But, on the other hand, once we know that there were approximately 25.000 persons in and around the Tuzla area after the finalisation of the deportation process out of Srebrenica, as well as a column of approximately 15.000 persons among which the 5th Corps said that 6.000 succeeded to arrive in BiH territory, that we have from the Red Cross approximately 8.000 missing persons, we end up roughly at the number I told and in the fork of the figures that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Srebrenica was a place from which people, civilians, preferred to flee if they had the chance than to move into Srebrenica during the time it was a protected area? In other words, do you agree that from 1994 onwards, that figure only dropped? It certainly did not increase.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the hellish living conditions that were imposed on these people from 1992 through 1995, the fact is that any reasonable brain person would only have one intention, if he's not wearing a camouflage uniform, so mainly the women, the children, and the elderly, would be to flee out of this area. But this does not change the figures that we just discussed previously. Anyhow, not significantly. The figures I -- I was talking about are the figures of July 1995, and again all what happened before, though it might be of interest for the, in brackets, ambience, is not something that was part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, what I'm trying to say, in fact my case is that during 1994, the population peaked. There were many more people than in July 1995 when the population was 37.000. Do you know that several thousand managed to flee, some with the UNHCR, others by breaking out individually towards Zepa, Serbia or Central Bosnia? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I don't know the figures. You say several thousand. I cannot confirm or infirm what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the evidence we've heard is that some people left with UNHCR in 1993, not 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was indeed 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is my case that people were leaving all the time and wanted to leave all the time throughout. I don't know if you've heard about it. If not, we'll show you documents. My case is that the population could not have been higher than in July 1994. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I really don't care. I only care about what happened to the 8.000 missing persons. The rest is not - I repeat it and I will repeat it again - not part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I am challenging your figure of 8.000, and I'm trying to prove it wrong. Do you know that in this courtroom commanders of the Dutch Battalion confirmed that they had 20.000 people in Potocari, whereas 13- to 15.000 went to the woods in order to flee towards Tuzla? You have to pay attention to that, because you are presenting a figure that I'm contesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could I have a citation to the Dutch Battalion commanders who said there were 20.000 people in Potocari in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember. What did Mr. Franken say about the number of refugees in Potocari, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head, Mr. President. That's why I was asking for a citation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in a document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue then, Mr. Ruez. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President Karadzic, we do not disagree on these figures. We don't disagree on these figures. Major Franken might have assessed the crowd, which is very hard to assess. Somewhere in open fields, some were inside buildings. So it's always a very difficult task to assess numbers. What we know more or less for sure was -- is that 25.000 people ended up in and around Tuzla in refugee camps. The figure of approximately 5 -- 15.000 persons in the column is also an assessment. No one could -- didn't -- no one counted them one by one. But if on this column of 15.000, 6.000 members of the 28th Division were at the spearhead that broke through the lines at Konjevici made it to -- made it alive despite of having had indeed also combat casualties in Tuzla, you have more or less the figure. And I'm not the person to challenge regarding the figure of 8.000. You should challenge the ICRC who created this list. The only important aspect of this list for the investigation is that it lists the names and the place where these people have disappeared from. And this is later on a very useful list in order to identify people, and once these people were identified by DNA inside the graves, we could take some sample of cases in order to take from the person who last saw the victim, to take what I named last-seen-alive statement, so that we don't only have the name on the missing book, but we also have the statement of the person who saw this victim alive and can say, for example, I was in a factory, Energoinvest, with Ramo and Ramo wanted to get onboard of a bus but he was separated. It's an example I invent at this moment, but this is the way we also made the connection between living people and then rotten flesh in mass graves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, Mr. Mitchell, on his feet, so I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did want to come back to this, because it's again something inaccurate has been -- was put to the witness. What Mr. Franken actually said, he was read a document which said: "There is more than 20.000 people in and around the compound." This is at transcript page 23162. And then Colonel Franken said: "I don't know how they came to the number of 20.000. Estimates are estimates and never very accurate." So can we please be accurate when we're citing to the testimony of other witnesses or documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Mitchell, but that was a comment on the contemporaneous document of the United Nations created in July 1995. That document refers to a figure of 20.000 plus, and the estimates at that time were more accurate than they are now after so much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you said Dutch Battalion commander confirmed that they had 2 -- 20.000 people. Be precise. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, he confirmed. That was written in a document. He said something more, but I showed him a document which refers to a figure of 20.000. It was a contemporaneous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then refer to that UN document, not a UN commander. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 20596.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give an interview to a parliamentary commission in France on the 22nd February, 2001?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was requested to testify. It was a common information mission from both Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the French parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see that document, please. We don't need the map any more. [No interpretation]: [In English] "the objective today is basically to remind you on the facts." [Interpretation] That's what you say in line 2 about the events after July 1995. That was what the interview was about; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview was about the reconstruction of the facts, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see page 3, please. Look here where you say in paragraph 2:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "many small-scale executions, individual or in small groups occurred in the area." [Interpretation] Did you establish when that began and how it proceeded? Was it also a consequence of mutual killing in the period before?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, line 4. I don't see this in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. No. With the Kravica -- yeah. In fact, many small-call -- yes. Absolutely, yes. Yes, absolutely. We don't go through this other, in brackets, small-scale executions. These parts of the book had been taken off by the Prosecution since President Karadzic was not indicted for these, in bracket, small-scale executions in the area of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but how did you understand these small-scale executions, if you'd like to call them that.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I -- I do not speculate on the reasons why people have been murdered at that spot, but if you say that it's revenge due to the consequence of mutual killings, I think you might very well be -- you might be very right on the motivation of these assassins. It could be indeed some revenge thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down you say that on the 14th of July, in the morning, the first detention centre, a hangar, there were 50 or so people who were killed with blunt instruments. [In English] Was evacuated. [Interpretation] And then it was evacuated. Do you mean Kravica? The warehouse in Kravica --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the hangar. The second paragraph is 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph are you talking about, and what line or part of line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second paragraph, line 2.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is the Kravica -- Kravica warehouse, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it exactly the way you put it here?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have been more precise, but that was not the goal of this -- this presentation. The execution at the Kravica warehouse did not happen in -- in one single event. It was more complex than that, if one can say. First execution of the people in the west part took place and in several waves. You have or will have the testimonies of survivors -- or survivor in this part. This is also the reason why it was important to determine if when Colonel Borovcanin and the -- the journalist, Zoran Petrovic, arrived on the spot that the execution was still ongoing, because it happened in several waves. They even called for survivors inside, telling them that the Red Cross had arrived and was present, and those who were still alive and went out, the survivor could hear shots being fired. So it was more a long process than what I say in these two lines, because it's only after all those executed in the west part were considered as dead that then the shooters executed the other prisoners on the other side. And meanwhile they were killing the people in one part of the warehouse, they were telling to the others that they were under attack from the hill so to keep them calm while being assassinated at that turn -- at their turn. But I didn't get into all these details even during the cross, but we could provide much more details during your -- your examination than during the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were very few guards there, that the atmosphere was relaxed, that a prisoner walked up to the guard to light his cigarette and in the process he snatched his rifle, he killed the guard and started shooting around? Do you know about that? Did you hear about that event?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about an incident, indeed, where a prisoner grabbed the gun of a guard, and could be that -- could be true. I think one guard also had his hand burned by the barrel of his gun. But in any case, due to the description I just made previously of the method of the slaughter in this house, even if this incident would be true and that a short panic occurred that could maybe even explain that several other prisoners might have suffered collateral damage when this rebelled prisoner grabbed the gun, it would in no case be an explanation for the systematic killing of absolutely all the prisoners from the east and the west part of the warehouse since the killing only stopped once the executioners were sure that no one had survived their activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, with all due respect, we have to leave something for the Trial Chamber. Let the Trial Chamber make conclusions. Let's, the two of us, establish how things were. Is it true that as soon as the warehouse was full the Serbs started shooting, or was it the way I described it? The atmosphere was relaxed. One of the prisoners walked up to a guard, he grabbed his rifle and continued shooting and that that incident was actually what triggered the course of events and leave everything else to the Chamber. I just need to know from you whether this was the chain of events that you were able to establish for that day.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not at all the chain of events that I heard. We know only two survivors of this slaughter at the Kravica warehouse. I don't want to speak in their name because I bet that they will come and explain the situation to the Court, but I never heard any of them telling that they felt invited at a tea party at the Kravica warehouse. So the relaxed ambiance, I leave that to you. I didn't say I believe that to you, I said leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, do you know that Kravica is the place where the Serbs were massacred on the 7th of January, 1993, which was the Orthodox Christmas, and that events -- event also played a role in the overall outcome? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the attack that was launched from inside the enclave during the Orthodox Christmas on the village of Kravica. This is also a reason why when we went to the Kravica warehouse during one of the missions there we also went inside the village of Kravica, since there was a possible doubt about the use of the facility, hangar style, inside the Kravica village as a possible execution site. But though this structure, like many of the houses inside Kravica, were severely damaged, we didn't find any evidence that the warehouse inside Kravica village had been used for any execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that neither you nor I should justify things or establish things? Let us just look into the following: Do you accept that the trigger for that shooting was the event that I described?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept it, because even though this event could be really confirmed, it doesn't change the reality of the situation that occurred at that location, which is a systematic killing of every single man who was within this warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what we should leave to the Trial Chamber. This is the only thing that I'm asking you now: Before that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, because you asked the opinion of the witness, the witness answered, gave his opinion. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking him for his opinion on that event. I'm asking whether that actually happened, whether this was the thing that triggered that event, the grabbing of the weapon from the guard, did that happen or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez answered that he heard of the incident, and whether it triggered something or not, you're asking -- inviting his opinion, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you said here that the killings in Cerska occurred on the 13th. However, that is not derived from this interview. It seems to have been later, right, on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the interview of the witness who was above the hill, the witness was above the hill when he saw the three buses escorted by one APCs in front of and one at the back of this little convoy, and then later saw the excavator entering the valley. This was on 13. And the one who managed to cross in this area and spotted the -- the pool of blood, it was during the night between 13 and 14. So this execution took place on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did they leave Bratunac? Did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, they didn't leave Bratunac at all. These people were either from the soccer field or from the 65th Protection Regiment. On the photograph from above at the 65th -- 65th Protection Regiment, there are three buses to be seen on the picture. I do not say that these three buses are the three buses we talk about in the Cerska Valley, but it indicates at the minimum that buses were there to take -- to take away, maybe to Kladanj, the prisoners who were inside the 65th protection compound, Protection Regiment compound. So these people in Cerska, I would not think they come from Bratunac, but everything is possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can we then establish who these people were? This man saw buses but did not see any execution; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I explained when we went through this crime scene, the witness could not see the execution. The exhumation uncovered 150 bodies with hands attached in the back and some of them even had their feet attached. These ones were most certainly not battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at page 4, what you say further on. So on the same day, on the 14th, a bus with 150 people on board arrived there and then there was the excavator. That's the 14th. And then further on you say the evacuation continued during the day of the 15th of July. You're referring to schools here, Pilica and so on. However, in the fifth paragraph you say: [In English] "In fact, however, the executions did not begin until the next day, 16th of July." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. The execution -- there were so many people in Bratunac that it took two days to evacuate them all. 14 July is the executions at the Orahovac and -- area, and the -- the barrage at Karakaj. The 15 is the executions of those at Rocevic, at the Kozluk site, and the 16th is the execution of those at the Kula school and at the Branjevo Farm, as well as the execution at the Pilica Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say here that about 1.200 people were killed; right? That's the paragraph in the middle. Between 1000 and 1500 hours at Branjevo. And then further on, you talk about this execution quad and: [In English] "... on the site and executed a number of people estimated by a member of the execution squad to have been 1.200." [Interpreted] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. The person who provides the assessment of 1.200 at the Branjevo Farm being Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you get anything more objective and impartial than Drazen Erdemovic? Could you not deal with it more scientifically, if you will?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Considering that possibly 1.200 were killed at the Branjevo Farm, that the figure of those slaughtered at the Pilica Dom was assessed by the security officer as being 500, we end up with 1.700. The only way to ascertain scientifically, as you say, these numbers is to add the number of bodies that were left at the Branjevo Farm, add this number to all the -- I mean to the nine secondary graves of Cancari valley which are connected through various scientific means to the primary grave of Branjevo, and add all these numbers that would then provide a precise number of executed people. I don't know yet if the full exhumation process of these secondary graves have been completed, but if this is the case, you will have scientific assessment that we all wish to have. If not, we will have an estimate that is not completed yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time to take a break now, if it is convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for 20 minutes and resume at 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now please focus on the rest. February 2000, that was the date of this interview; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 5 now. Please take a look at the fifth paragraph starting from the top: [In English] "The minimum number of individuals exhumed to date is 2.028. It is a very much reduced figure, and it is the minimum number of individuals determined by the pathologists during the autopsies. It will be possible to make this figure more precise when all the exhumations have been completed and will certainly be higher." [Interpretation] Today you said that if we do not confirm that, it remains an estimate only. In 2001, you have a total of 2.028 exhumed. That is the minimum number, as you say; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So within this number of exhumed individuals, did you establish who were the individuals that had been killed in fighting in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the persons that were exhumed in these graves connected with the detention sites from -- in which the prisoners coming from Bratunac had been buried has a connection with combatants. All these were unarmed prisoners. And now we are in 2012. This is why the figure has considerably expanded, and in between these 11 years, 10 years, the DNA identification has taken place. Unfortunately, still today I know that the full exhumation process is, unfortunately, not completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, a moment ago you confirmed that DNA analysis did not say anything in terms of time of death or mode of death; right? The fact that DNA analysis was carried out does not show that these persons were killed in fighting or that they were victims of an execution. I'm not talking about people whose hands had been tied. How did you establish that they had nothing to do with fighting?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed this is not a DNA identification that provides the information about origins of the dead. Nevertheless, this part is done by other aspects of the investigation when you reconstruct the path followed by these people from detention site Bratunac to detention site in the area north, and all these people in the graves are those who were in these various detention sites. The analysis of the graves, as I said, will be detailed by Dean Manning, and you will then have a very clear and detailed view of this step-by-step process, from the surface of the grave to the inside of the grave and then to the secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were the combat casualties buried in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know. I repeat, we were not looking for combat casualties but to identify the detention sites, the nearby execution sites, and the successive burial places of these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, how many people died in combat during those few days in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To know that precisely, we would again have to finalise the full exhumation process of the sites connected with the assassination of the prisoners and retrieve this number from the total number of those reported missing to the ICRC. This will give an indication of those who have an unknown cause of death. This unknown cause will then be considered, even if it is not necessarily the case, as combat casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see that list of the ICRC, the list of persons who arrived in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am talking about the ICRC list of missing persons in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you mentioned that the Red Cross established how many had arrived in Tuzla, 25.000; right? That's what you said today.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25.000 is not the -- is not necessarily an assessment of the Red Cross. It's the assessment that was made of the people who were inside refugee camps inside and around Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is not reliable information coming from the Red Cross, that only 25.000 got out; right? It is the estimate of those who were in refugee camps; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- I don't remember precisely the source regarding these refugees in and around Tuzla. It could also be the Red Cross. It could be also the UN who was there. It was also -- possibly also the assessment of the Bosniak authorities, and also we have to add, as I said, the 6.000, which was a number given by the BiH 5th Corps as being the number of those of the 28th Division who made it through Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think or do you have information that all the refugees were placed in refugee camps around Tuzla, or were some put up with their families, relatives who lived there? Were those who were put up in private accommodation included in the total figure?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could very well be, but again I need to refocus on the fact that the only number of real concern for the investigation is the number of those who are on the ICRC list of missing persons and who were missing from Srebrenica July 1995. So the figure of around 8.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm challenging that, sir. There's no way of confirming that. Let us now look at what the 2nd Corps reported on the 16th of July. 1D -- actually, D1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that. I do apologise to Mr. Mitchell, because I had sent another number in the notification. So this is what I'd like to have in e-court, D1998. I will go back to this document. Next page, please. I beg your pardon. Actually, can we still look at this and can we see the bottom of the page. This is the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is the security administration. This is an official bulletin. The date is the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we had an English translation. That's why it's admitted in full without being marked for identification, with the understanding that the English translation to be uploaded by Defence, but I don't see the English translation yet which has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that that is the case. We'll see now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is not, it is a fault on the part of the Defence. I think the thing was that the Prosecution offered the English translation at the time. But in the meantime, let us proceed. Or can you proceed with other topic while the Registry -- either the Registry or the Prosecution can assist you with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps that would be better. Can we go back to the previous document, then, 20596.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the bottom of the page, of the first page. Let's move to the bottom of the first page. Your response was that on the 11th of July, 1995, and I'm going to proceed in English because I believe that the interpretation will be better: [In English] "All the military and civilian leaders of the enclave realised that it was going to fall. The population decided to go in two directions. All the able-bodied men, which was most of them, gathered in an area of the enclave and in the night of 11 to 12 ... began to leave the enclave one by one in a column and crossed the minefield in order," can we get another, "to take the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road and then climb up the Cerska Valley and escape in that direction." [Interpretation] So you had the information that almost all able-bodied men joined the convoy, the breakthrough convoy; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I explained previously during the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second direction that you mentioned was about civilians, women, and elderly who decided to proceed towards Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you can imagine during the testimony, the Assembly, the need to enter details is not so thorough that in a courtroom. The fact is that able men were also in Potocari, and you can even see them on the videos available, filmed at that date in Potocari by Zoran Petrovic, as well as the men that were walking from the white house towards buses. So there were also an X number of able men in Potocari who were then taken to Bratunac, the 12 and the 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 5 again. You say here in the penultimate paragraph, in the last sentence, you say: [In English] "In the end there will probably be more than 4.000 people whom we will be able to say were executed in cold blood in this organised and systematic procedure." [Interpretation] Do you still believe that the 2.028 were victims of the execution, and was your estimate that there will be more of them, exactly the same number of them?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of 2.028 is the number of those who were exhumed by 2001. Since the exhumation process was very far from being completed in 2001, it was a certainty that the figure would raise very significantly, but since the press was constantly talking about 8.000 people killed though no one really can know what this figure would really be since we need to complete fully the exhumations to have this final number, I used the figure of 4 as a very conservative number that would be reached. And we can see now that it was very conservative, because though the full exhumation process is not over, there are already now some 6.000 people identified by name through DNA and on the missing list as missing since July 1995 from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you believe that the 6.000 whose DNA was established, that they were executed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those found in the graves, the primary and the secondary, have all been assassinated, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we will show you that this is not correct. Let's look at page 6. At the top you say this: [In English] "Thus there are all those who died in fighting and those who committed suicide. The only figure to be kept in mind is that of those who were arrested, detained, transferred, executed and will probably rise to 4.000 to 2.000 people after all the exhumations." [Interpretation] On the following page, you increase the figure to 5.000. Do you know how many of the 6.000 who were identified died before July 1995 were killed before July 1995 in various places?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, those who were found in the primary graves and in the secondary graves which are connected with the primary graves, they all went through the detention process, Bratunac and the area north, and all these people are not combat casualties. They have all been gone through the extermination process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will look at what Muslims themselves say about that. And now in the third paragraph you say: [In English] "Paramilitaries were involved in this matter. In fact, Arkan did not take part in the operation." [Interpretation] Did you establish what kind of paramilitaries could be seen moving about that area?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the reason for this comment about Arkan is that one UN observer who had served at one point at the Croatian front where he had seen Arkan men wearing black uniforms believed that when he saw the beginning of the attack where the 10th Sabotage Detachment took place, he thought that men in black were Arkan people, where we know now that they most certainly were members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, which is a regular unit of the Bosnian Serb Army and not any paramilitaries coming from Serbia. One of the killers originated from -- originating from Bratunac who took part at the execution at the Branjevo Farm, though he was from Bratunac, was in fact from a, in bracket, paramilitary unit of Bijeljina, and he happened to be in Bratunac on leave during when the enclave fall, and he volunteered to -- to join for the executions. So it's not a paramilitary operation. It's the units of the Drina Corps who took part in the execution process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we go to page 8. You were asked about the difference between civilians and soldiers, and you answered. You said that this was used by the Serbian propaganda, and you said that actually every individual, every able-bodied man could be considered a combatant in that context. And you go on to say that the existence of 5.000 infantry weapons and pieces means that there were 5.000 combatants. Do you know that our war was waged in three shifts, and if there was a lack of rifles, the rifle would remain being used in combat, but they were used by different people?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The reason why I -- I talked about this is that as you very well know, and I will assist you on that, there was a mobilisation order just before the enclave fell. So due to this mobilisation order, every able man could be very well considered as a combatant. The point is that due to the chain of events since all these people at one point ended up being either captured or for most of them just surrendered, at the moment they surrender they are supposed to be under not only the custody but the protection of those who captured or received them in surrender. Since after that we enter the process of a cold-blooded assassination of all of them, the fact that they are military or civilians does not matter any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're trying to establish facts. We're not trying to give them any meaning. Let's stick to the facts. Did you confirm here the people who surrendered, who came out of the woods, threw their weapons prior to surrendering, because that was safer for them. You will find that in the third or fourth line from the bottom. It's in the last paragraph, lines 2 and 3: "[In English] Most of the men got rid of their weapons before surrendering." [Interpretation] Is that correct? Right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the people were jammed on top of these hills on 13 July, they were called by the Bosnian Serb forces along the road with megaphones, where they received security guarantees, hearing that, ICRC is here. The UN is here. Come down. No one will harm you. And they could see, indeed, blue helmets on the road. The fact is that we also could determine that there was no UN personnel on this road. There was no ICRC. These people were ruled by a tricky method by Bosnian Serb soldiers who were wearing these helmets disguised as UN personnel. So the sense of security in a way can be considered in such a context as being extremely relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ruez, we could see just one young lad in that clip, and he was the only one bearing a blue helmet. How can you claim that Serbs -- all the Serbs wore blue helmets everywhere? Are you claiming that, and when you claiming that, do you have in mind only that one lad with the blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one you call a lad is a Bosnian Serb soldier wearing a camouflage uniform and has on his head a stolen UN blue helmet. I don't say, because the witnesses don't say, that all the Bosnian Serb soldiers were wearing these helmets, blue helmets. Only a few had such helmets on the head. This is what the witnesses say. But these few were enough of them to believe that the security guarantees they were receiving were genuine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? Are you a mind reader? How do you know things that were in the heads of other people?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when you interview these people, they tell you what they had in the head at the moment they report to the -- to a investigators, what they have seen and what they have heard. And when you then have a film taken by a journalist who was together with the Bosnian Serb Army and then you can get a visual confirmation that what they said was no fantasy because you have one obvious evidence of truth and are your eyes, you end up believing that what they told you is indeed not a fantasy but a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that the Registry got the English translation of that bulletin thanks to the co-operation of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence submitted that on the 12th of January, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at your response in the lower half of the page. Thank you. Francois Lamy asks you: [In English] "Do you have evidence that there was any possible planning before the massacre?" [Interpretation] Your response: [In English] "No, there is no evidence of prior planning. In fact, it was not planned to take the enclave. The operation plans for the offensive was dated 5th of July. I think that the air defence component of the operation was dated 6th or 7th of July. It is possible to have an exact date. The decision to take over the enclave was not made until 9th of July when General Mladic realised that the enclave would not be defended. The initial objective was to reduce the enclave to the town of Srebrenica and transform it into a huge open-air refugee camp to force the United Nations to evacuate the zone." [Interpretation] Mr. Ruez, is this a bit of an exaggeration? Was the first and only task before the 9th and 10th of July to separate Srebrenica from Zepa and to regain the control of the road that belonged to us between Srebrenica and Zepa? You say that there was a limited task to reduce, and so on and so forth. Do you know that the safe area had its borders that were previously agreed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The knowledge that we had at that time and leads to what I said at the commission is written black on -- black on white in the Krivaja 95 operation plan. The goal was to reduce, not to take fully the enclave. To reduce it, if I remember well the phrasing, in such a way to make the living conditions so unbearable that the place would have to be evacuated. More details about this plan will be most certainly provided to this Chamber by the military analyst who worked on all these captured documents, Richard Butler. As far as the planning of the one I call extermination process, more information was learned about this after my departure in 2001. So I might not be the relevant person to talk about it. Richard Butler might also be able to provide more details on the planning of the actual --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise. I have to stop you here. The process to reduce the enclave, are you saying that the Serbian plan was to reduce the enclave to an extent below the agreement, and do you agree that the enclave had previously been enlarged by the Muslims beyond the agreed borders and that's how they managed to cut our road between the two enclaves? Can you answer that, or perhaps we should leave that to Butler as well?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The debate is not indeed part of the investigation, but, yes, these lines were moving. The BiH claims that each time there was a switch between the battalions, the UN battalions, the Serb side used the opportunity to reduce the size of the area. The Serbs, they indeed say that the Bosniaks were willing to cut the road going from -- making the tour from Zeleni Jadar to Milici, and so on. But at the end of the day, what we know for sure is that the entire enclave, the entire UN safe area was overwhelmed by the Bosnian Serb forces, as was Zepa, and that all of this was part of a finalisation of eradicating these spots embedded in Serb-held territory. So this is the broad picture. It's not the goal of the investigation to enter in these aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now display but not broadcast transcript page 22674. My thesis, Mr. Ruez, is this: Many graves that were dug in 1995 pre-existed that time, and that this sanitisation process affected those graves, that there are no other graves. They're all the same graves. Let's see what was said about that here by one of the Muslim survivors. 22674 is the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have tens of transcripts. What transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the date? Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's 10th of January this year, day 228, and it's KDZ045.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the question: [In English] "And how" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I would like to be sure whether we can stay in open session. Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This was in public session, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is confirmed by the Registry. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can believe me, Mr. Ruez, that Witness 045 is a Muslim who survived the breakthrough. On line 3, it says: [In English] "They were serious throughout the whole period." It means attacks. "There was shelling ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think that's a huge misrepresentation of this witness's evidence. This is a witness who survived an execution at the dam, not a witness who survived the breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to line 1 on page 22674. My question was: "Were these serious attacks ..."? And he says that "they were serious throughout that whole period," the whole breakthrough period. This was before he was actually captured. He speaks about numerous casualties, about 40 to 50 people who were wounded, and he also speaks about those who died. There were so many killed that nobody could carry them out from the creek. They carried those who were wounded. They -- they did not carry the fallen. And we're talking only about the 281st Brigade, and he says that -- actually, I asked him on page 22: [In English] "Did you bury the people who had been killed in the fighting in these -- Potoci?" In this area. "A. ... it's a bit of a silly question, if I may say that. How could we have time to bury anyone when you don't even know what will happen to you the next minute? We didn't even have time to look at anyone." [Interpretation] Can we move to the following page. [In English] "Q. Who buried these people?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "A. Nobody ever did unless they were found later or the Serbs gathered them and put them in mass graves. All the rest are probably still there in those woods." [Interpretation] So you say that everything in the mass graves were victims of executions, whereas this man who was on the spot saw his friends falling next to him. He names several combatants who got killed near him, and he said that mostly nobody buried them from the Muslims, that the Serbs picked them up and latter put them in mass graves. Did you take this into account?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am on your question on the transcript. So, yes, absolutely. Can we have "yes, absolutely," on the transcript as being my word. The reason why I say yes, absolutely is that we know as a fact since it's in the records of the Bosnian Serb Army, in the records of the Engineer Unit of the 1st Zvornik Brigade that the heavy equipment used to bury the bodies was already on the spot at Orahovac when the execution took place and that this initial burial of the victims on this execution site occurred on 15 July, that then it moved to the Karakaj dam where it buried the bodies of those killed at the dam. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Don't interrupt. Please continue, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the digging of the bodies at Kozluk occurred also on 15, that the execution that took place at the Branjevo Farm and the Pilica Dom on 15, exhumation was done on 16 by the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Unit, and that all this exhumation work was finalised on 17, and this is when the security officer of the Drina Corps, Vujadin -- Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic could make his report to Colonel Beara, saying that this entire operation deserved an A rate. So this leaves little room to try to think that the bodies of those left around in the combat area had ever been transported to these execution sites to be mixed with the bodies of those who did not die in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By exhumation on line 14, you meant a burial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Inhumation, yes, inhumation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your assumption is that those victims or casualties along the column were not buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many were probably left around. As an example, at the Orahovac site when going towards this little dump site, there was a skeleton in civilian clothes lying along the dirt path. A peasant was rolling on it in the morning and in the evening every day since long. No one ever collected his bones. He was certainly not a Serb victim. He was probably someone who crawled away of this area but didn't make it more than a hundred metres approximately. So bodies indeed were left around, and the battle casualties close to the front lines were most probably indeed buried in mass graves with these military casualties just nearby the place where they were collected. There was -- is no need in such circumstances to transport the bodies far away from the place where they are found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you have these separate graves where combatants were buried on video footage?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about the graves where sanitation operation led to bury combatants in mass graves, nor did I see when you started this piece of your examination you reproduced orally something that I am supposed having said - I don't know in what circumstance - and which is -- I don't recognise through the transcript that I could read on the screen anything I had previously said, so I would like to maybe return on this small paragraph which don't make much sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this page, 49, line 8. You suggest that all combatants got killed during the breakthrough of the 28th Division and that they were all buried next to the place where they died. Do aerial photographs show that, because if they were buried, if earth was dug, then that also would have been noticeable.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about this part. I'm talking about the part at the beginning of this part of your examination where you say that I said that graves are pre-dug in 1995, pre-existed. I mean, something I have no remembrance having ever said in my life. If we could return on this part, that would be maybe useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While page 40 is still on the screen, do you stand by what you said in line 8, that you believe that those who got killed during the breakthrough were not buried together with the victims of executions but were buried instead, as you've said on lines 8, 9, and 10, were buried close to the spot in separate graves?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I totally agree with this, yes. The graves we have exhumed have nothing to do with combat casualties. I was just referring to another paragraph where there is no document on the screen, at least not at this moment, where I allegedly said that the graves we dug -- we dug pre-existed. This is a part of something that you said at the very beginning of this phase of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I did not describe that to you. I'm asking you now where are those graves that you mention where those who got killed during the breakthrough were separately buried? Why didn't the aerial photographs identify them when they identified every change on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have to explain how aerial imagery can be used. Every image represents a large square. Without talking about the type of aerial platform that enabled to take the pictures we have shown, you can see on a very open source documentary named -- Discovery Channel named "Spies From Above" the functioning of a year 60 old plane named U2, the one that photographed the Cuban missiles. It's a photograph of a square 30 kilometres long and north/south, in which you can then zoom towards a spot to have a close shot of this specific spot. So when on this large piece of ground you have indeed a lot of information, in order to pinpoint the information, you need to have an indication that leads you to this specific spot. The pictures we did request, when we were asking for any type of aerial imagery, was always of a very specific area. So this is how we got the imagery. The reason why we do not have imagery of suspect areas that could be connected with burial of battle casualties has a simple reason. We, in the course of this investigation, had no reason to go after graves that were mass graves of the so-called cleansing of the terrain that is done after combat. We only focus on areas where we know prisoners were taken to, executed, and buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you wanted to ask -- comment on Mr. Karadzic's question or comment. It's transcript page end of 35 and 36. I will read it for you. This is what Mr. Karadzic said: "Could we now display but not broadcast transcript," this one, "My thesis, Mr. Ruez is this," I'm quoting, "many graves that were dug in 1995 pre-existed that time, and that this sanitisation process affected those graves, that there are no other graves. They are all the same graves." You wanted to comment on this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand now. I thought that Mr. Karadzic was referring to any -- something I might -- I might have said. Now I understand that it is his thesis. I thought he was putting this in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that apart from interviews with survivors, you were guided by aerial imagery to spots which show changes on the surface; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. It is correct at one point. The chronology is simple. All the primary graves, we were not directed by imagery to these spots --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm asking you how you used the images, how you excluded changes on the surface resulting from combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you first hear him out and then ask supplemental question. He was -- he was trying to answer your question. Please continue, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's answering a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. Please continue, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer President Karadzic's question, I explained the two things. First phase, the primary graves. We were not oriented by aerial imagery. We requested, based on the information we had, access to imagery of very specific spots. Based then on this imagery, we could find very precisely the spots we were trying to identify. For the second phase, the secondary graves, aside the graves in Zeleni Jadar when it was based on ICTY request Office of the Prosecutor to access to imagery, the rest of the sites, the Cancari sites, the Hodzici sites, the Liplje sites, we were directed to these sites by work done by others, and that we went then to the spots in order to make a first dig and assess these secondary graves. So it's two phases, one phase where we were directing the providers on certain pictures. Second phase, where we were directed by the providers. And again to answer the other part of the question of the defendant, we did not request any -- we did not pinpoint any area where could be mass graves with battle casualties, because these battle casualties were completely out of the frame of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see again this 20596, page 11. Look at this. You are asked here where the first images were taken and how you used them. You say: "[In English] We have no photograph at all showing the execution taking place if that is what you wish to know. We always have photographs showing before and after." [Interpretation] So you are guided by changes on the surface shown by aerial photographs; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On those photographs, how many spots of disturbed earth were there where you concluded you didn't need to dig because they might only contain casualties of combat?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none of them, since the spots we -- on which we requested comparison before and after were spots to where we were guided by the reconstruction of the events based on the witness testimonies. So none of the spots we were requesting imagery had a connection with combat casualties since the persons who were taken there were prisoners, not combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say a moment ago that a Muslim who was involved in both the breakthrough and the executions said that they had left behind many of their dead who were later buried by the Serbs into mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're just repeating your question. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if he's going to quote, we might need to go back to that transcript so it can be exactly accurate. He didn't -- that survivor didn't say the dead were later buried. He said they may have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Unless," [Interpretation] he said, which means if they didn't bury them, we certainly didn't. Mr. Ruez, how many people, to the best of your knowledge were buried during the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. These people are not part of the criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fine, but you are aware that some got killed in the minefield; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some got killed in various activities linked with combat. This investigation is not about war -- warfare. It's about a massive assassination operation, nothing to do with combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you personally find evidence that in one locality more than 600 got killed in combat and this locality is called Bare? Do you have any knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mass grave nearby Bare is the one I was talking about when we heard indeed that there was a mass grave near Bare. Knowing this mass grave was containing battle casualties, we did not consider even going to this spot. Battle casualties are not in the frame of a criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of fact that Mrs. Elizabeth Rehn personally toured the area and saw hundreds of bodies of combat casualties? Are you aware of the existence of some film about it, a documentary?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
